title: Observability, SLOs and Incident Basics: Quick Revision
summary: Night-before revision notes on logs, metrics and traces, golden signals, SLIs, SLOs and error budgets, alerting, rollback versus roll forward, and incident response basics. Ends with a one-page cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Logs, Metrics and Traces: The Mental Model
points: Observability means you can explain unknown failures from the outside using emitted telemetry. Monitoring only checks known failure conditions.

Logs are timestamped event records that give detail on one event. Metrics are numeric time series that are cheap and aggregatable. Traces follow one request across services as spans with a shared trace ID.
Comparison: metrics tell you THAT something is wrong, traces tell you WHERE, and logs tell you WHY. Metrics are cheapest to store; logs are the most expensive at volume.
Mistake: using high-cardinality values (user ID, request ID) as metric labels. This explodes the number of time series and the cost. Put those in logs and traces instead.

Interview Point: What is the difference between monitoring and observability? Why do metrics not replace logs? What is a trace ID and how does it propagate between services? What is label cardinality and why does it hurt?

chapters.title: The Four Golden Signals
points: The four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors and saturation. They are the minimum dashboard for any user-facing service.
Latency is the time to serve a request. Track it separately for successes and failures, because a fast error response hides real slowness. Traffic is demand, such as requests per second.

Errors are the rate of failed requests, including explicit 5xx responses, wrong content, and responses that are too slow. Saturation is how full the most constrained resource is (CPU, memory, disk, connection pool, queue depth).
Comparison: RED (rate, errors, duration) suits request-driven services. USE (utilization, saturation, errors) suits resources like hosts and disks.
Mistake: alerting on average latency. Averages hide the slow tail, so use percentiles (p95, p99). Example: a p99 of 3s with a mean of 120ms still means 1 in 100 users waits 3s.
Interview Point: Name the four golden signals and give an example of each. Why use p99 instead of the mean? What is the difference between RED and USE? What does saturation mean for a queue?

chapters.title: SLIs, SLOs and Error Budgets
points: An SLI is a measured ratio of good events to valid events, for example successful requests divided by total requests. An SLO is the target for that SLI over a window, for example 99.9% over 30 days. An SLA is a contract with consequences for missing it.
Error budget = 100% minus the SLO. A 99.9% SLO over 30 days allows about 43 minutes of downtime. 99.99% allows about 4.3 minutes.
Burn rate is how fast you spend the budget. A burn rate of 1 uses the whole budget exactly at the end of the window. A burn rate of 10 empties it in a tenth of the window.
Policy: when the budget is healthy, ship features faster. When it is spent, freeze risky releases and put the work into reliability. Set the internal SLO tighter than the SLA.
Mistake: aiming for 100%. It is unachievable, and the cost of each extra nine rises steeply. Choose SLIs that reflect what users feel, not server CPU.
Interview Point: How do SLI, SLO and SLA differ? Calculate the monthly downtime allowed by 99.9%. What is an error budget used for? What is burn rate?

chapters.title: Alerting That Pages the Right Human
points: Alert on symptoms users feel (error rate, latency, SLO burn), not causes (CPU at 80%). Page only when a human must act now. Everything else becomes a ticket or a dashboard item.

Multi-window burn-rate alerting: page when the 1h and 5m burn rates are both above about 14x (about 2% of the budget gone in an hour). Open a ticket for a slow burn of around 1x over 3 days. The short window makes the alert reset quickly after recovery.
Comparison: a threshold alert (value > X) is simple but noisy. A burn-rate alert is tied to the SLO and tolerates brief spikes. Use a `for:` duration so a single blip does not fire.

Example Prometheus rule: `alert: HighErrorRate`, `expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) > 0.01`, `for: 5m`, with a runbook link in the annotations.
Mistake: alert fatigue from noisy, non-actionable pages. Every alert needs a clear owner and a runbook. Delete or demote alerts nobody acts on.
Interview Point: Why alert on symptoms rather than causes? What is a multi-window burn-rate alert? What makes an alert actionable? How do you reduce alert fatigue?

chapters.title: Rollback vs Roll Forward and Incident Basics
points: Rollback redeploys the last known good version. Roll forward ships a new fix on top of the bad release. Default to rollback when a recent deploy caused the incident, because it is fast and predictable. Mitigate first and find the root cause later.

Roll forward when rollback is unsafe: an irreversible database migration, data already written in a new format, or a fix that is a one-line change and quicker than a redeploy. Backward-compatible (expand/contract) migrations and feature flags keep rollback possible.

Incident roles: the incident commander coordinates and decides, the ops lead fixes, and the comms lead updates stakeholders. Declare a severity (SEV1 is full outage) and keep one shared channel and timeline. Everyday commands: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/api`, `kubectl rollout status deployment/api`, `kubectl logs deploy/api --since=15m`, `git revert <sha>`.

Blameless postmortem: timeline, impact, root cause and contributing factors, what went well, and action items with owners and dates. Judge the system, not the person. Track MTTD (detect), MTTA (acknowledge) and MTTR (recover).

Mistake: debugging live before mitigating. Stop the customer impact first by rolling back, failing over, or toggling a flag. Another mistake is a rollback that was never tested, or one that skips the schema change.
Interview Point: When do you roll forward instead of rolling back? What does an incident commander do? What goes into a blameless postmortem? Why mitigate before finding the root cause?

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Observability, SLOs and Incidents
points: Pillars: metrics say THAT, traces say WHERE, logs say WHY. Keep high-cardinality values out of metric labels. Golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. Use p95/p99, not the mean.
SLO math: error budget = 100% - SLO. 99.9% over 30 days is about 43 min. 99.99% is about 4.3 min. Burn rate 1 spends the whole budget over the window. SLA is looser than SLO.
Alerting: page on symptoms and SLO burn only. Pair a long and a short window (1h and 5m at about 14x) and use `for:`. Every page needs a runbook and an owner.
Deploy failure: rollback by default (`kubectl rollout undo deployment/api`), roll forward only if rollback is unsafe. Use expand/contract migrations and feature flags.
Incident flow: declare severity, assign commander, mitigate first, communicate, then write a blameless postmortem. Track MTTD, MTTA and MTTR.
Interview Point: Walk through an outage from the first alert to the postmortem. How would you set an SLO for a new service? What would you put on a dashboard for it?
